review_text_clean: [b]DISCLAIMER: I was provided a press review copy for the purposes of documenting the game for PCGamingWiki, a publicly-editable technical wiki for games.[/b] What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into [i]anything[/i]? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything. [b]TL;DR:[/b] It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time. [h1]Is this Uplink 2.0?[/h1] For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is [i]not[/i] the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because: [list] [*] You use a 'real' computer with fixed specs, with HacknetOS running on top of it as a VM (Virtual Machine). [*] The game is command-line based with some GUI helpers, such as an IP map, optional GUI-based system navigation, and a note app. [*] You can only run computer-compromising apps via command-line. [*] The game's story, despite being subtle, in the background, and without limitations (i.e. x number of connections before game over), drives the game, and your actions are ultimately in service of the story. [/list] If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO... [h1]Gameplay[/h1] As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is [i]very[/i] careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier. The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old. Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end. [b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b] You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter. All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time. Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles. [h1]Story[/h1] I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with. [h1]Graphics[/h1] The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you. [h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1] I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

review_text_raw:
This game is good. Just not great.

I actually didn't finish this game, but I read a story synopsis and it was, well, not too creative. Decent, but not amazing. The reason I didn't finish is because the story effectively takes a break for about 8-10 hours after the first hour, having you invest into smaller stories that you come across in small missions. The other reason I didn't finish was that the gameplay felt like actual hacking and work, and it was the kind of grindy, difficult work that one might receive in a classroom. Some features of the UI were extremely difficult to operate, and while that was somewhat realistic, I came to play a game, not because I liked doing difficult computer work, which is part of the reason why some hackers become hackers. Speaking of that, this game makes hacking extremely easy and simplified. I guess that if a hacking OS was developed in real life, it may actually be this easy, but in reality now hacking is way more difficult, complicated and sometimes more fun than this.

The world building and details were fantastic. I can't tell you how many times I laughed scrolling through logs on PCs I'd hacked into. They were well written and funny. But the massive break from the story made me feel like I was actually doing hacker work (although way too easy) and not playing a game. I came to experience a story, play a game, be something and someone else for a while, not to actually do hacker work. This game did not advertise as a hacker sim, but as a game where you play as a hacker with a story. That is my main problem with this game.

And don't get me wrong--I am all about games that require you do think and reflect and do not have big visuals or explosions or gunfights--this game's gameplay was boring. I've already said how the hacking was too easy and the UI was way too hard, but simply, hacking got boring rather quickly. That's basically it. In terms of additional information, there were no bugs and it was programmed very solidly. 

Overall, get this game when it is very cheap and play it for a few hours. You can have more fun with it than just two hours, so you don't have to return it, just buy it very cheap or free, that's how I got this game, it was free for a limited time and I downloaded it. 79/100 -- good, just not a B.

review_text_raw:
The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

review_text_raw:
The game's unique mechanics and addictive storyline make it an absolute pleasure to play.

One of the things I love most about Hacknet is how immersive it is. The game does an incredible job of making you feel like a real hacker with its realistic interface and authentic hacking commands. It's a game that not only entertains but also educates on the intricacies of hacking.

The gameplay itself is challenging but rewarding. Each mission requires careful planning and execution, forcing you to think outside the box to achieve your goals. And the game never feels too difficult, thanks to its clever hint system that guides you in the right direction without giving away the answer entirely.

But what really sets Hacknet apart is its history. The game tells a compelling narrative that will keep you hooked from start to finish. The characters are well developed and the plot twists are brilliant. By the end of the game I was emotionally involved in the outcome of the story.

Overall, Hacknet is an excellent game that I would recommend to anyone who loves hacking or puzzle games. It offers a unique and immersive experience not to be missed.

review_text_raw:
[h1][b]IF YOU LIKE THE IDEA OF A GAME FOCUSING ENTIRELY ON A TERMINAL/COMMAND-LINE AND SOME EASY TO MODERATELY DIFFICULT PUZZLES THROWN IN, YOU MAY LIKE THIS GAME.[/b][/h1]
As someone who has a bit of experience with the UNIX terminal and commands, this game had my absolute full attention and felt familiar to me. [b]I've just recently bought this game (yesterday, at the time of writing) and I was absolutely HOOKED and couldn't get away from it. Hacknet is absolutely my style of game! (right now, I've just beaten the base game and will go through the DLC content shortly. but I may fiddle around with the Extensions)[/b]

[h1][b]TARGET[/b][/h1]
Obviously, this game isn't for everyone. A terminal-based game can seem intimidating or uninteresting to someone who has no experience with it before (and even if you do, a terminal-based game may not be that interesting). If the screenshots and description provided by the game do not capture your attention, it's probably not the game for you. But if your curiosity is piqued, it may be a great experience for you.

[h1][b]PUZZLE ELEMENTS AND TUTORIALS[/b][/h1]
Hacknet introduces itself quite well to the uninformed, and doesn't hand-hold. It throws you straight in after a short tutorial on using the terminal and interface, therefore encouraging experimentation with what you have available. By not holding the player's hand, succeeding in the puzzles without any additional help besides what the game provides will give you a sense of accomplishment. However, that can turn some people off, and if it does, it may not be for you.

It is possible to get stuck in several points in the game, but no solution is too far out there and is solvable without a walkthrough. (and I admit, I have, and have consulted a walkthrough but I was extra careful not to look any further ahead than the current task at hand, most of the time I had just forgotten something simple and was able to get back on track quickly).

The puzzles start off pretty easy, leading you on and increasing the difficulty as it goes, pretty much gently guiding you on how to work with the game's unique nature.

At certain times, the tasks can seem repetitive, and to be fair, it is. You are constantly trying to break into a lot of different computers, servers, devices, etc. but that's what it is. It is an accurate representation instead of the flashy Hollywood style hacking seen on film (but it certainly can be flashy when it wants to be and is for certain parts).

[h1][b]STORY[/b][/h1]
The story itself is nothing outstanding, but it certainly fits the theme and style of the game. It's perfect for the game. The story is there for the beginning and the end of your gameplay, giving you purpose to start and an objective to reach near the end. In the middle of the game, you are given freedom to do what you wish. Or PointClicker, if that's your thing (I won't judge!).

[h1][b]MUSIC[/b][/h1]
The music is an absolute fit for Hacknet and I often found myself focusing on the killer beats rather than what's at hand. It also made me quite shaky during the parts that are time-based.

[h1][b]OVERALL[/b][/h1]
Overall, Hacknet is extremely accurate compared to other things that have tried to display this kind of topic before. The elements work wonderfully and the balance between gameplay and the real elements is on point (all the commands given are used at one point or another and no unnecessary garbage is there). To the average person who may not know anything about the terminal, it can be exciting to get into it for the first time not knowing anything and eventually learn (there may be a little higher risk of getting stuck at a point, but that's okay!). To those who are a little familiar with the terminal and commands, you'll feel right at home and understand the game quickly and have a great time with it!

[h1][b]SHOULD YOU GET IT?[/b][/h1]

[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
I have a confession.

I like goofy fake hacking scenes in movies.

I know it's not indicative of "actual" hacking, and as a programmer I should probably be a little miffed at how unrealistic they make the whole thing seem. But I don't care! I love it anyway.

Hacknet promised to give me that kind of feeling, and like Uplink before it, it kinda did. It's a puzzle game where your tools are 'hacking programs' and your problems relate to breaking into computers and grabbing info, deleting info, or causing chaos.

It works well, and it reveals just how satisfying it is to solve software problems, even when it's heavily abstracted and simplified.

But my biggest problem with Hacknet is that it never really takes that next step into something greater than a simplified hacking game. Toward the end of the game there's a distinct feeling of "That was it?"

Want to hack an SSH port? Then use SSHportHack.exe. Want to hack an FTP port? Then use FTPportHack.exe. The entire game is like this. For each problem or situation there's almost always exactly one answer, and there are few opportunities to feel clever. 

In some ways the game actually feels unfinished. Many computers you hack into contain generically named folders that are either empty or have snippets of IRC conversations from Bash.org. The game is set in modern times, yet your computer only has ~800mb of RAM and you can never upgrade it. The UI for selecting systems to hack into is an absolute nightmare.

There are even mechanics that don't seem to actually...exist? For example, a big deal is made about deleting your logs and leaving no trace behind - a classic hacking trope - yet I never once saw any consequences for forgetting. I eventually just stopped clearing logs and it never was a problem

As I said, I like Hackers-style hacking. It's fun and goofy and still scratches the same itch as actual hacking. Hacknet gets close, but its far too shallow and misses the mark.

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

So yeah. This game left me absolutely speechless. At 2AM. Ending sent shivers down my spine. And there's waaay more. Whilst decrypting one of the files i decided to check out its header. There was an IP of a server. It was NOT related to the mission. I wasn't even suposed to check the header. I wasn't curious or patient enough to follow this lead but it was there. The author of the game sates that every person we meet in the game CAN BE TRACKED DOWN!!! I trust him. 

Hacknet is a simulator situated really close to real hacking - true, but it's also something way bigger. It's an epic story. A possibility for a player to enforce the type of gameplay he desires. Yes - you can cooperate with a hacking group but in the meantime you can hack their server and read their personal e-mails. 

Don't get me wrong - this game is linear. You can't get to other endings. You can't make other people react to your actions. Even when you intentionally send a guy p.e: wrong password - he won't respond. Only "Mission incompleted" window will pop up. It's not even like the player thinks he can make the world respond - you don't have any illusion of sandbox. 

Still tough. The Game left me thinking. Not about the story of Bit. Not about the story of V. Not even about the genius of the maker, nooo... I was thinking: "What the hell am I going to do with my life now?". I am amazed. I am mesmerized. I approve. Brown, out!

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

Good:

    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

I'm not entirely sure what the target demographic is for this game. It's an ostensibly terminal-based game running on a UNIX platform, but it has minimal overlap with bash commands, and trying to treat it like bash will only get you confused. 

So, this must be aimed at people without any tech background. However, how much fun can someone uninterested enough in coding to not care about this have, if all they're doing is typing in the same auto-completing commands over and over into a terminal?

Oh, and you can't scroll on the terminal, too. On the other hand, the GUI is both cluttered and unintuitive. Everything feels horrid to use.

It claims to feature "REAL HACKING", but the hacking consists of running magic hack spells via the terminal, and, if you DO know anything about hacking, that makes a lot of what the game asks of you feel obtuse. It took me so long to realise that I was supposed to open up a shell on my own PC, which, if crashed, would somehow take down a proxy server hosted elsewhere? I was assuming I had to find some kind of initial access mechanism to bypass the proxy and execute shellcode on the target PC, but, uh, I guess crashing the equivalent of cmd.exe on my computer really is the future of hacking.

The story is okay, I guess. At least it was easy to 100%.

My advice to anyone interested in a hacking-type game aimed at beginners is to check out the (free!) OverTheWire Bandit wargame, instead; it's fun, and it'll actually teach you something useful.

Hacknet is an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC. Dive down a rabbit hoIe as you follow the instructions of a recently deceased hacker, whose death may not have been the accident the media reports. Using old school command prompts and real hacking processes, you’ll solve the mystery with minimal hand-holding and a rich world full of secrets to explore.

Bit, a hacker responsible for creating the most invasive security system on the planet, is dead. When he fails to reconnect to his system for 14 days, his failsafe kicks in, sending instructions in automated emails to a lone user. As that user, it’s up to you to unravel the mystery and ensure that Hacknet-OS doesn't fall into the wrong hands.

Exploring the volatile nature of personal privacy, the prevalence of corporate greed, and the hidden powers of hackers on the internet, Hacknet delivers a true hacking simulation, while offering a support system that allows total beginners get a grasp of the real-world applications and commands found throughout the game.

There are clear influences from Uplink, but Hacknet stands on its own two feet for many design decisions.

Hacknet requires a lot of typing due to the text console. This brings a level of realism which is enjoyable, and the countdown timers do not seem to require the player to type at 200 words per minute. However, a few actions can also be initiated by mouse using a graphical user interface. The use of the mouse is a bit incoherent: those features which can use the mouse and those which cannot feel arbitrary and without obvious design merit.

There are a number of little bugs here and there. Head over to the discussions and check the bug report thread. Many of the valid bugs reported actually have more to do with polish. It's unfair to call them bugs, but fixing the issues could enhance the game's polish and lead to better immersion. There are a few actual bugs that can lead to gameplay issues, but they seem to be few and far between.

The story is a bit linear. I have found it hard to explore the networked universe outside where the missions take me. Compare this to Uplink, where there are a great many ways to find and access computers by goofing around. Computers tend to have random snippets from bash.org , which are humorous logs of conversations that reportedly happened on IRC. It's a nice touch as a reward for looking at systems and it makes them feel a little more fleshed out, yet the contents tend to be disconnected from any of the game's context. The snippets simultaneously help and hurt immersion.

Creative expression is available in small doses, but I do not consider this any kind of sandbox game. The potential for such a thing is there. For example, there are computers which run web servers. You can modify the HTML, and when you visit the web server, your changes are visible. It can be amusing to deface a virtual server even if no other living being will see it. However, if you delete all the system files from a computer and then forcibly shut it down, it should prevent the system from rebooting. This would destroy a system. In Hacknet, if you do this, the system will disappear from your network map for a little while and then come back (while still lacking system files). As a related polish-bug: you can immediately connect to any computer "destroyed" this way using the command console, even if the network map does not show the system as online.

The music is electronica-themed to suit the stereotype of a computer hacker. The sound track brings good ambience. I personally start to notice the repetitious nature of the music after playing 2-3 solid hours, but that's usually a good time to take a break anyway.

The recent release for Linux/Mac is welcome, except that has introduced a number of new bugs that need to be squashed. Save game interoperability is a current problem that needs to be resolved at the time of this writing. Linux/Mac support has its own thread in the game's Steam discussion area. I'm sure those problems will be resolved soon enough, but they are worth reading through before purchasing if you plan to play on Mac or Linux.

Overall, I'd say Hacknet is a fun puzzle game with a solid computer hacker theme. It could use more polish and the design decisions regarding keyboard or mouse interfacing could use some rethinking. As a professional programmer and IT person, I cannot really say with certainty if this game is accessible to non-programmers or non-IT people. I suspect the game is approachable enough to anyone who has ever had to type commands into anything instead of clicking glittery UI buttons.

review_text_raw:
While this game is being sold as a "hacking simulator", a debate will likely rage about what exactly it simulates. In either case, it comes suspiciously close to being a realistic simulation of hacking. So close, in fact, I'm left wondering why the dev didn't go the extra yards to make it inarguably so (maybe something he can shoot for in the future). Realism nit-picking aside, this game is full of very realistic nods to hacker and IRC culture, and in broad strokes, represents some of what goes on in actual exploits. While the experience of compromising systems is streamlined for the sake of keeping it an actual game (again, is it a puzzle game or a simulator?), in that "push a button, get bacon" sort of way you see in "hacker" movies, there was still much in the game that reminded me of taking the OSCP (for those who know my pain, you will find much in each mission to make you smile in that corpse-like rictus you had while laughing at emails and files during enumeration pratice in the Offsec lab).

After a while, I realized I was playing not so much because of the faux-hacking experience, but because there was a rather compelling story unfolding. Can't pick that apart without spoiling it, so I'll critique the gameplay instead (positives first):

[b]Pros:[/b]
This game is hilarious in a sick, twisted way. References to chan and IRC culture litter the storyline. While the majority of gameplay involves limited exploit combinations, there are moments where you don't know what the f**k is going on, and you have to think fast to avert a crisis. If you're into security culture, you'll find your intuition meshes well with the challenges, and you can improv what to do most of the time. It's like a Drunk History version of real hacking, so it's probably an ideal game to play while you're drunk.

People with zero knowledge of hacker culture or basic unix commands and quad notation will walk away familiar with all of the above.

The game is cheap, so whether you enjoy the simplistic, repetitive nature of the "hacking" it simulates, you won't regret the purchase, because it will entertain you regardless. The story itself is worth the price, and the way the story is told using the genre is clever.

If you liked TIS-100 (and I'm a recovering TIS-addict) you'll appreciate this for some of the same reasons, but the games aren't identical by a long shot. In fact, that would be the one constructive criticism I'd like both devs of these two games to hear: if TIS-100 had the narrative of Hacknet, and Hacknet had the coding fatures and complexity of TIS-100, you'd have a seriously ground breaking game on your hands, guys.

[i]Maybe the two of you should consider a collab or something...[/i]

[b]Cons:[/b]

Pushing buttons to get bacon gets fairly boring after a while, and the game loses some of its puzzle quality attributes as a result of the limited attack combinations, and the lack of customization or tweaking of exploits and tactics that is the real joy of hacking. If this was never going to be a hacking game, and more of a puzzle game, I wanted to see a complexity progression throughout, instead of a chaotic difficulty plataeu. 

[b]Also, why write so many missions for lelzsec, but make it so easy to permanently lose your chance to access them -- it was like a quarter of the game just gets skipped automagically because there isn't a clear choice presented to the player that an alternate path exists![/b]

Each mission certainly could have involved more manual hacks to achieve both realism and puzzle difficulty, but this would require adding more OS commands to the game, or a limited scripting engine of some sort. It couldn't have been that hard to add a mission where the solution was to exploit weak service permissions, tampering with programs launched by the OS at boot. Perhaps telling the print spooler to reset the system's admin password by re-writing it to launch a file with a "passwd" command in it, or to add a user account with "admin" privileges, something along these lines. A phishing mission, or getting a target to open an email and trigger a malicious trojan embedded in a PDF file would have been fun. These kinds of scenarios would require no "hacking tools", and might actually require the player to struggle. I'd rather struggle than push "exploit" over and over, my only real enemy being the trace timer.

To do this would require more system commands like "touch", privileges to edit, the ability to create files, maybe a basic word processor and the ability to write emails (instead of just reply... to some of them). All we had to work with were pre-existing files, a "replace" command that replaces lines and is too cumbersome, and no manner of scripting available. No complex chains of commands, no writing or editing code beyond some HTML (so I can change "chicken" to "c**ks", but that's not really hacking as much as being a d**k).

Once you get to that long slog of a valley mid-game, it stops feeling like hacking AND puzzle solving, and starts to feel more like grinding mobs in an MMO to get to the next bit of storyline. Each player will have more or less patience for that experience. Exploit tactics become routine too quickly, and the difficulty drops off.

[b]OVERALL[/b]:
Short game. In 20 hours you can play through twice and get all the achievements, and you compulsively will, despite the bugs that might force you to start a new game because something is glitched and can't recover [though the developer is working hard to patch all these, props to him]. There are enough Easter Eggs and humorous logs to make you anxious that you missed some the first time. More like an interactive novel for hackers than a puzzle game or simulator, but with elements of both; you will feel haunted putting together what your *actual* role in the missions might have been, and to what extent the Ayy Lmaos were involved. 

For $8-ish, I felt like I got more than I paid for and told my friends to play it for the lulz.

review_text_raw:
I have been waiting for the game to start, and now that I'm halfway through I've given up. It's boring and pointless. There is no story, there are no choices (even though the game wants you to think there are). That aside, it's not really a hacking game. "Hacking" just means typing the same commands and waiting for them to execute... every time... for every PC in the network.

Another big problem is that the game implies that it will use real world logic but then it doesn't. Like I can't execute a file on a PC I'm connected to? Since when? 

Instructions are never clear and even if they are I hate that the game forces me to only do things how the dev intended. Specifically for advcancing missions, it's never clear whether I just need to read the file or send it or send the password contained in it. All of those should work, not just one!

There are bugs - mostly soft locks, which is unacceptable for such a simple game.

Instead of spending time on the visualizations for each tool the dev should have spent time designing mechanics around them. For instance the firewall analyzer is okay. Not fun, but it's not completely idle, you have to do something. Each tool has to be like that, there has to be some mini-game associated with it, or there has to be some strategy as to which tools are used in what order.

I don't know what the music was like. It was so repeptitve so annoying I turned it off and played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines OST. 

The only thing I liked about the game is the environmental storytelling. The chat logs sound EXACTLY like the Old Internet days. Kudos to the author for the research!
